groups.label: Platonic & Historical Polities
groups.summary: This sequence examines political philosophy and ideal states, tracing the development from Plato's own works to later historical traditions. It begins with reflections on simplicity in law and medicine, transitions through comparative analyses of Platonic dialogues, and surveys successive visions of governance across Roman, medieval, and Renaissance thought.
groups.rationale: All entries come from introductory commentary comparing Plato's political theories across dialogues (Republic, Laws, Statesman) and evaluating later philosophical and utopian traditions (Cicero, Augustine, Dante, More, Campanella).

groups.label: Early Conceptions of Justice
groups.summary: In the opening dialogue, Cephalus reflects on character in old age and the comfort of wealth in avoiding unpaid debts and transgressions. Socrates challenges these practical views with counterexamples about returning property and interrogates whether rulers can mistakenly legislate to their own disadvantage.
groups.rationale: These sections cover the early dialectical exchanges in Book I regarding traditional definitions of virtue, wealth, and justice between Cephalus, Socrates, and Thrasymachus.

groups.label: Socratic Aporia and Reflection
groups.summary: Concluding the first book, an editorial note and Socrates' own confession describe his dissatisfaction with the preceding exchange. He laments having pursued ancillary inquiries into the profitability of justice before defining its fundamental nature, ending in complete uncertainty.
groups.rationale: Both items directly record the conclusion of Book I where Socrates reaches an impasse (aporia) and expresses self-criticism over the course of the argument.

groups.label: Adeimantus on Justice Itself
groups.summary: Adeimantus critiques conventional praises of justice that emphasize only external reputation, worldly rewards, and divine favor. He challenges Socrates to set aside these superficial motives and demonstrate how justice and injustice inherently affect the soul of the possessor.
groups.rationale: A contiguous pair of passages in Book II wherein Adeimantus formulates his two-part challenge to redefine and defend justice based strictly on its intrinsic nature.

groups.label: Guardian Education and Statecraft
groups.summary: Socrates establishes regulations for the city's guardians, requiring the censorship of terrifying underworld myths to cultivate courage against death. In tandem, truth is praised as a standard, reserving deceit strictly as a medicinal prerogative for magistrates acting on behalf of the public good.
groups.rationale: Both entries address Book III discussions on shaping the character of the guardian class through myth regulation and political authority.
